description: We're building Zero-G Guide, an AI astronaut trainer assistant that guides users on their journey to space. It creates personalized training plans, tracks physical and mental health, and offers real-time coaching for microgravity and long-duration missions. Our goal is to make astronaut-level preparation more accessible, data-driven, and safe.
summary: A ten-day Moon or Mars outpost game. One decision a day, two choices, three bars. Every choice costs air, power or radiation, and the solar-storm day is priced against live NOAA space-weather data.
details:
What it does and how it works

Play starts with a choice of base. Mars is labelled Easier (radiation ×1.0) and the Moon Harder (×1.3), because the Moon has no atmosphere to absorb particles. The player then works through ten day-cards. Each card states a problem in one sentence the base is cold, dust covers the solar panels, a rock sample looks strange and offers two actions. Every action carries visible effect chips (air, power, radiation, science report), so the price of a decision is known before it is taken, not after. On top of the chosen action the base charges a fixed daily cost of 5 air and 3 power for life support and heat.

The deck holds fourteen cards. Ten are drawn per run: the solar-storm card always falls on day 5, the moonquake card appears only on the Moon, the dust-devil card only on Mars, and the remaining cards are shuffled and partly omitted, so two runs are never identical. Radiation accumulates and is capped at 100. Optional science reports give the win a second dimension: surviving with none reads "The crew survived. Earth learned nothing," while three or more reads "The crew made it. Full science."

The live-data hook

The solar-storm card is the one card whose numbers change with the real Sun. The app reads NOAA SWPC GOES X-ray flares and ≥10 MeV integral proton flux before play. If proton flux is at or above the 10 pfu S1 threshold, or an X-class flare has just occurred, the card's radiation exposure rises by 90% and the card says so, quoting the measured value. Otherwise the card explains that the Sun is quiet but particles are forecast. If the feed is unreachable the interface says so and falls back to the forecast rather than inventing a number.

Depth for older players

The mission console reuses the same NOAA feeds plus the planetary K index and SWPC alerts to produce a ranked advisory log, each entry carrying its evidence, source and three numbered crew actions. One-way light time to Mars and the Moon is computed from low-precision orbital elements at the speed of light. A radiation screen tracks career dose against the ~600 mSv limit with per-source shielding transmission. Eight checklists cover fire, depressurization, CO₂ rise, solar particle event, power failure, medical emergency, comm blackout and dust storm.

Tools and languages

React 18, Vite 6, Tailwind CSS v4, plain JavaScript. Frontend only, no server, no login, static deployment under 250 kB. NASA data via EPIC, the JPL rover photos API and the NASA Image and Video Library; partner data via NOAA SWPC and wheretheiss.at.

Creativity and factors considered

Most space-weather demos show a dashboard. This one turns the same measurements into a decision a nine-year-old can make and defend. Balance was tuned by simulation: always picking the first option wins about 35% of runs, always the second about 75%, random play about 82%, and reading the trade-offs about 100%, so attention is rewarded and a single blind habit is not. Rate limits and offline behavior are handled with a five-minute cache and honest unavailable states. No NASA logos or branding are used, and SI use is disclosed below.
